settings.title: Firmest at the ankle
settings.text: Pressure is highest where fluid pools first after a long day on your feet.

settings.title: Easing through the calf
settings.text: It eases off up the calf, working with the muscle that pumps blood back up the leg.

settings.heading: Pressure that climbs the right way
settings.text: A compression sock only works if the pressure is graded: firmest at the ankle, lighter as it climbs. Get the gradient wrong and it is just a tight sock. That grading is what an orthotist checks on every Vital design.

settings.text: Vital Socks was started by an orthotist who measures and fits medical compression garments for her patients. She knows what the wrong pressure does to a leg, so she oversees the compression grading on every Vital design.

settings.question: What does graduated compression mean?
settings.answer: The sock is firmest at the ankle and gets gradually lighter up the leg. That gradient helps move blood and fluid back up towards the heart instead of letting it pool in the lower legs.

settings.question: Which compression level do I need?
settings.answer: Every product page states its compression range in mmHg. Lighter ranges suit everyday wear, travel and long shifts. If you have a circulation condition, diabetes or a history of blood clots, speak to a healthcare professional before wearing compression.

settings.question: How do I find my size?
settings.answer: Measure your ankle at its narrowest point and your calf at its widest, ideally in the morning. The fit finder turns those two numbers into a size. Shoe size alone isn't enough, because compression depends on the leg.

settings.question: Who shouldn't wear compression socks?
settings.answer: People with peripheral arterial disease, fragile or broken skin on the legs, or reduced feeling in the feet should not wear compression without medical advice. If in doubt, ask your doctor or an orthotist first.
